Now I understand the issue! Let me trace through the failing test to confirm my hypothesis:

Looking at `test_lru()` line 23: `cache[2]` - this is a read operation.

The problem is in the `LRUCache.__getitem__` method (lines 294-295). It calls `cache_getitem(self, key)` which retrieves the value, but it does NOT call `self.__touch(key)` to mark it as recently used. 

The `__touch` method is only called in `__setitem__` (line 299), which marks items as recently used when they are written, but not when they are read.

The `get()` method in the Cache parent class (line 121-125) also calls `self[key]` which would trigger `__getitem__`, so it also doesn't mark items as recently used.

Perfect! I can see that `LFUCache.__getitem__` (lines 225-229) calls `self.__touch(key)` after retrieving the value, but `LRUCache.__getitem__` (lines 294-295) does not!

This is the bug. The `LRUCache.__getitem__` method should call `self.__touch(key)` to mark the key as recently used when it's accessed.

## Hypothesis

**File:** `src/cachetools/__init__.py`

**Function:** `LRUCache.__getitem__` (lines 294-295)

**Cause:** The `__getitem__` method doesn't call `__touch(key)` when retrieving an existing item. This means reading an item doesn't mark it as recently used. Only writes (via `__setitem__`) mark items as recently used. As a result, the cache behaves like FIFO instead of LRU.

**Fix:** Modify `LRUCache.__getitem__` to call `self.__touch(key)` after retrieving the value, similar to how `LFUCache.__getitem__` does it. This will ensure that accessing an item marks it as recently used.
